verses.note: Judgment begins with the tempter. God does not treat the serpent as a partner to be reasoned with; he condemns it outright. Isaiah's vision of the new creation keeps this sentence in force, with dust as the serpent's food even when wolf and lamb feed together (Isaiah 65:25).

Death is presented as God's sentence on sin, the unmaking of what 2:7 made. Scripture keeps this verse's words (Psalm 90:3, Ecclesiastes 3:20) and treats death as an enemy, the last to be destroyed (1 Corinthians 15:26).

Exclusion from the tree of life is judgment, but many readers have seen mercy in it as well: endless life in a state of sin and alienation would be no gift. The tree reappears in Revelation, open to those who have been washed (Revelation 22:14).

Innocent blood has a voice before God even when no human court hears it. Scripture repeats the theme in the souls under the altar crying for justice (Revelation 6:9-10), and Hebrews sets Christ's blood beside Abel's as speaking a better word (Hebrews 12:24).

The punishment fits the crime: the man who poured blood into the ground loses the ground's yield. Scripture repeatedly pictures bloodshed as polluting the land (Numbers 35:33), so that violence against people is also a wound to creation.

The longest life in Scripture still ends in death, and it ends at the threshold of the flood. Length of days is a blessing, but it does not escape the sentence on sin. Psalm 90:4 sets even a thousand years beside God's eternity as a day that has passed.

Judgment arrives with a delay. Whether the 120 years limit lifespan or count down to the flood, God sets a bound rather than acting at once, and Peter reads the time before the flood as God waiting patiently while the ark was built.

The judgment includes the animals, because humanity's rule over creation (1:28) means creation shares humanity's ruin. Paul makes the same connection in reverse when he says creation waits for the redemption of God's children (Romans 8:19-21).

Before God announces judgment, the text establishes that the world has already destroyed itself. The prophets use chamas for the injustice that brings judgment on Israel's own cities (Amos 3:10, Habakkuk 1:2-3).

Even at this point God gives seven days' notice. The delay does not change the verdict, but it shows judgment arriving on a stated schedule after warning, which Peter reads as God's patience while the ark was prepared (1 Peter 3:20).

The mountains, Scripture's image of what is stable and lasting (Psalm 90:2), are covered. Psalm 104:6 describes the waters standing above the mountains at creation before God's rebuke drove them back; here the rebuke is withdrawn and the waters return.

The breath God gave in 2:7 is withdrawn. Death is presented not as nature taking its course but as the Giver of life taking back what he gave (Job 34:14-15). Jesus uses these days as the pattern for the suddenness of final judgment (Luke 17:26-27).

The promise limits the form of judgment, not judgment itself. Scripture continues to speak of God judging the world, and 2 Peter 3:5-7 sets the flood beside a future judgment by fire. What the covenant rules out is another undoing of creation by water, which gives history the stable ground on which God's saving purposes will unfold.

God's judgment here is preventive. He acts not because the tower is a threat to him, but because a united humanity set on its own name would pile up evil, as it did before the flood. The restraint of sin is itself a mercy.

The name of the world's proudest city becomes a monument to God's judgment. The prophets later speak of Babylon's fall in similar terms (Isaiah 13:19; Jeremiah 51:53), and Revelation uses Babylon as the name for every power that sets itself against God.
The plagues on Egypt are promised as judgment, a verdict on a nation that enslaved and afflicted God's people. The exodus is not arbitrary power but justice for the oppressed.

God will not give Abram's family a land whose inhabitants have not yet deserved to lose it. The conquest is presented as judgment on accumulated sin, delayed for generations, and Leviticus 18:24-28 holds Israel to the same standard.
To refuse the sign is to refuse the covenant. The verse shows that the covenant's grace is not indifferent to a response; the one who rejects the gift is cut off from the people who have it.

God's judgment answers a cry. The outcry language is that of victims crying for help (Exodus 3:7-9), so the coming judgment on Sodom is presented as God's response to the oppressed, and he examines the evidence before he acts.

The title Judge of all the earth makes Sodom's fate a matter for the God who judges every nation, not a local deity's grudge. Paul makes a similar argument when he asks how, if God were unjust, he could judge the world (Romans 3:5-6).

The few righteous can be the reason for sparing the many. Jeremiah 5:1 later offers pardon to Jerusalem if one just person can be found, and the principle points toward the one righteous man whose obedience brings life to many (Romans 5:19).

The narrator's insistence that every man, young and old, joined the crowd shows the judgment falling on a city whose wrong has become common practice. The investigation of 18:21 is answered by the city's own conduct.

The angels say the LORD has sent them to destroy the city, and verse 24 says the LORD rained fire. Scripture often speaks of God's judgments carried out by angels (2 Samuel 24:16, 2 Kings 19:35) while treating them as God's own act.

‘I cannot do anything until you reach it’ shows the principle Abraham appealed to in 18:25 at work: the Judge of all the earth will not sweep away the righteous with the wicked. The fire waits until Lot is safe.

Sulfur and fire become Scripture's standard image of divine judgment, from Psalm 11:6 and Ezekiel 38:22 to the lake of fire in Revelation (Revelation 20:10, 21:8). Jesus uses this day to warn of the suddenness of his coming (Luke 17:29-30).

God treats the taking of another man's wife as deserving death even when the man who does it was deceived. The verse shows judgment as God's defense of the vulnerable, here Sarah, who has no one else to speak for her.

Punishment falls on every man of a town for one man's crime. Israel's law later insists that each person is put to death only for his own sin (Deuteronomy 24:16), and Jacob's deathbed words condemn the brothers' anger. Genesis refuses to call this justice.

The question has force, and the narrator leaves it hanging because the chapter's verdict comes later. When Jacob blesses his sons he judges this deed (49:5-7), and the Law and the Prophets will teach that justice for the wronged must not become a new injustice.
The text does not say what Er did. It is enough for the narrator that God saw it and judged it, which leaves the reader with a God who evaluates what no human court has examined.

The phrase “He put Onan to death as well” sets the two sons side by side. The chapter's first lesson is that the LORD takes the family's obligations to a vulnerable widow seriously enough to judge their violation with death.

Reuben believes that shed blood is never forgotten by God. The conviction reaches back to Abel's blood crying from the ground (4:10) and to the covenant with Noah (9:5-6). He is wrong that Joseph is dead but right that God holds people accountable.

The brothers' terror is the natural response of the guilty before the one they wronged, who now has full power over them. What follows shows judgment giving way to mercy, but the text does not skip the terror.

A single act, long unmentioned, is not forgotten. The verse shows judgment working through the natural consequence of unrestrained character: the man who could not govern himself does not govern his brothers.

The same sentence of scattering becomes loss for Simeon and blessing for Levi. God's judgment in Scripture is real, but it is not a fate that closes off his mercy; what a later generation does with the sentence matters.

Joseph does not deny that a wrong was done or that it deserves judgment. He denies that judgment is his to carry out. Paul makes the same move when he tells believers to leave room for God's wrath (Romans 12:19).

The order sets up a pattern of just recompense that runs through the book: the king who throws Israel's sons into the water loses his own firstborn son (12:29) and sees his army thrown into the sea (15:1, 4).

The judgment on Egypt's firstborn corresponds to Egypt's attack on God's firstborn. The last plague is presented as just recompense, announced in advance, with every opportunity for Pharaoh to avoid it.

The foremen appeal to God as judge, but against the wrong party. The scene shows how suffering can turn the oppressed against the very people God has sent to help them, a pattern that recurs in the wilderness (14:11-12; 16:3).

The judgment falls on persons and on powers at once. By striking the firstborn of Pharaoh, the heir of a god-king, the LORD shows that the gods Egypt trusted could not protect even their own. The verse makes the plague a verdict in a contest of sovereignty, not a random catastrophe.

The last plague answers the first act of oppression. Pharaoh ordered Israel's sons thrown into the Nile (1:22), and God had warned that because Pharaoh refused to release his firstborn son Israel, Pharaoh's own firstborn would die (4:22-23). The verse carries out a judgment announced long in advance and refused ten times.
God does not delegate this sentence. Eating blood is treated as an offense against God's own claim on life, and so God himself answers it.
The threat to destroy Israel ‘from the face of the earth’ is stated plainly. The covenant's blessings in the land carry covenant consequences, which the curses of Deuteronomy 28 will spell out.

Accountability follows revelation. Those to whom God has spoken are answerable for whether they listened, a principle the Letter to the Hebrews applies to God's speaking in his Son (Hebrews 2:1-3; 12:25).
God's answer to rebellion is first a word. His anger is not arbitrary rage but the response of rightful authority defied, and the psalm will still offer the rebels terms of peace (verses 10-12).

God's judgment on Edom is not favoritism toward Israel but the defense of what is his. The land is ‘My land’ (verse 5), and the jealousy that judged Israel for idolatry now burns against those who treat his judgment of Israel as their opportunity.

The books opened in God's court mean that the judgment of the powers is not arbitrary; it rests on a record. Scripture uses the image for God's knowledge of all deeds (Malachi 3:16; Revelation 20:12). For persecuted readers the point is comfort: nothing the beasts have done is unrecorded.

The fourth beast is destroyed, while the earlier ones lose their power but not their existence. Many interpreters see here the historical fact that conquered peoples survived their empires, and a theological one: God's judgment is measured, not indiscriminate. Revelation 19:20 draws on this verse for the beast thrown alive into the lake of fire.

The last word on the persecuting power is God's court, not the power's own boast. Judgment in Daniel is the necessary condition of the saints' reign: the kingdom cannot be given until the beast's dominion is taken away.
